events.text: The stair ends at a door that still smells of fresh lime. A clerk of {ln_court} looks at the dust on your hem, finds nothing written about you, and writes "from below" in a ledger with a column for nothing else. Behind the clerk, {ln_elder} is laughing at something. You are fairly sure it is you.

choices.text: Ask what the other columns are for

effects.log: There are none yet. The clerk is new here too, and blushes, and draws you a second column.

choices.text: Brush the dust off, slowly, in front of them all

effects.log: The laughing stops. The clerk underlines "from below" twice.

choices.text: Sit on the step and wait to be sent for

effects.log: Nobody sends. By evening you have noticed that the step is very well made, as if by someone who cared.

events.text: Nobody meets you. The gods of {ln_court} are at dinner, and a heaven this young has no porter yet. You sit in the outer hall beside {ln_peer}, who came up last spring and has still not been spoken to. "They think the ground sticks to us," {ln_peer} says, and looks at both your boots. "It does, a bit."

choices.text: Share the bread you carried up the stair

effects.log: {ln_peer} eats it in two bites. You have a friend in heaven, and crumbs on the floor of it.

choices.text: Walk into the dinner

ok.log: Somebody moves along the bench without looking up. It is not a welcome. It is room.

fail.log: A servant walks you back out by the elbow, kindly, as one walks out a goat.

events.text: A herald of {ln_court} has been sent to meet you, a minor one, still learning the forms. The herald reads out who you were, {ln_was}, gets it nearly right, and adds "of no account here" because it is written on the card. The gods along the cloud rail lean over to see what you will do with the card.

choices.text: Thank the herald for a fine reading

effects.log: The herald is so relieved that the next newcomer is given a kinder card.

choices.text: Ask for the card, and keep it

effects.log: You pin it up wherever you sleep. In a hundred years it will be funny. It is already slightly funny.

choices.text: Correct the herald, aloud

effects.log: Correct is not the same as welcome. The rail goes quiet and stays quiet.

events.text: The floor of {ln_court} gives slightly underfoot, like a bridge not yet walked on enough. {ln_elder}, one of its old seated ones, says you may lodge in the guest wing "for now", and hands you the list of things guests may not touch. It is a long list. Somebody has added your own name to the bottom of it.

choices.text: Read every line, twice

effects.log: You learn the rules of this heaven faster than anyone who came before you. It does not make you liked.

choices.text: Touch the first thing on the list

ok.log: It is a bell. It rings beautifully. {ln_elder} very nearly smiles.

fail.log: It is a bell. It does not stop ringing for a week, and everyone knows whose hand it was.

events.text: They know who you were. Word came up the stair ahead of you: {ln_was}. So {ln_court} has laid out a carpet, a short one, and stopped it a pace before the door, so that you will see exactly where it ends. {ln_elder} waits at the end of it with a smile cut to measure.

choices.text: Step off and walk the last pace yourself

effects.log: You walk it on bare cloud. {ln_elder} notes it, and the gods along the wall talk of nothing else for a month.

choices.text: Stop where it stops, and wait to be asked in

effects.log: You wait an hour. You are asked in, which in this heaven is not nothing.

choices.text: Roll the carpet up and carry it in

ok.log: Half the hall is outraged. The other half has to look away to keep from laughing, and it is the better half.

fail.log: The whole hall is outraged. Nobody is laughing but you.

events.text: A great name on the ground is a small name up here, and the gods of {ln_court} have decided to be gracious about it. You are given a seat at the high table, at the very end, beside the god of a river that dried up. The river god has not had a guest in a long time, and talks to you about water for the whole of the feast.

choices.text: Listen to the river god

effects.log: You learn more about this world in one evening than in a life below. The river god asks you back.

choices.text: Talk across the table to the powerful ones

ok.log: They answer, briefly. One of them remembers your name the next morning.

fail.log: They answer the river god instead, pointedly, about the weather.

events.text: In the long gallery of {ln_court} the portraits of the gods hang in the order they were seated. There is a nail at the end with nothing on it. A servant of {ln_order} tells you, cheerfully, that nails are for gods, and that the likeness of one from below goes in the corridor by the laundry, if it goes anywhere.

choices.text: Sit for a portrait anyway, for the laundry

effects.log: The laundry women adopt it. It becomes the best-kept picture in heaven.

choices.text: Hang your hat on the empty nail

effects.log: It is gone by morning, and so are you, in the eyes of the gallery.

choices.text: Walk past

effects.log: You walk past. The nail stays empty, waiting for somebody.

events.text: {ln_peer} has been here two years and is still seated below the salt, below the musicians and once, memorably, below a cat. Tonight the steward seats you below {ln_peer}. It is the first time {ln_peer} has ever been above anyone in heaven, and the joy of it is painful to watch.

choices.text: Let {ln_peer} have it

effects.log: {ln_peer} glows all night. In the morning a better blanket is waiting outside your door, unsigned.

choices.text: Offer to trade seats

effects.log: {ln_peer} refuses, accepts, then weeps. The steward writes you both down as trouble.

choices.text: Ask the steward where the cat sits now

effects.log: Above both of you, it turns out. The table laughs, and for once it is with you.

events.text: The gods of {ln_court} have a word for those who climb up from the ground: "dustborn". They never say it to your face. They say it just behind your face, at exactly the volume of a face. {ln_elder} says it twice in one morning, and then asks you to pass the ink.

choices.text: Pass the ink

effects.log: {ln_elder} writes something long and does not look up. That is the whole morning.

choices.text: Pass the ink, and say "dustborn" back, warmly

ok.log: {ln_elder} blinks, then laughs once, like a door coming unstuck.

fail.log: {ln_elder} does not laugh. The word is said a third time, more carefully.

choices.text: Ask what the gods themselves were made of

effects.log: Nobody answers. Several gods look at their own hands for the rest of the day.

events.text: A garden party in {ln_court}, and you are invited, in the sense that your name is on a second list pinned to the back of the first. At the gate a lesser god of hedges checks both lists, finds you on the back one, and sighs as though handed something heavy that will need watering.

choices.text: Go in by the back list

effects.log: You eat very well and are spoken to by nobody. The hedges are superb.

choices.text: Offer to help the hedge god with the lists

effects.log: By sunset the two lists are one list, in order. The hedge god will not forget it.

choices.text: Leave a flower at the gate and go

effects.log: Somebody carries the flower in. It ends up on the high table, and they wonder who sent it.

events.text: The bath-house of {ln_court} has three pools: one for gods, one for the heaven's own immortals, and one for others. The third is cold, and has a sign. A child of some seated house reads the sign aloud as you pass, and then again, in case the dust in your ears is thick.

choices.text: Bathe in the cold pool, singing

effects.log: It is very cold. You sing very well. Two immortals come to listen and stay to bathe.

choices.text: Chalk another sign beside it for the child

effects.log: You write "Water does not know who is in it." It stays up a week, and the child reads it aloud too.

choices.text: Go unwashed, on principle

effects.log: You go unwashed for a month. The principle can be smelled two halls away.

events.text: A list goes round of who may walk the upper terrace of {ln_court} at sunset. It is very short. {ln_peer} is on it by a slip of the copyist, and is so frightened of being found out that you are asked to come along, as a witness to nothing in particular.

choices.text: Walk the terrace with {ln_peer}

effects.log: Nobody stops you. The sunset is the finest this world has, and this world is not small.

choices.text: Tell the copyist, gently

effects.log: The copyist fixes it, and adds your name instead, out of gratitude. Then rubs it out, out of fear.

choices.text: Tell {ln_peer} to walk as if it were no mistake

ok.log: {ln_peer} walks like a god. By the next list it is no mistake at all.

fail.log: {ln_peer} walks like a thief, and is caught, and blames the sunset.

events.text: A seated god of {ln_court} sends you a gift: a cup with a crack in it, the kind given to a servant about to be let go. The courier who brings it does not know what it means. Everyone else does, and they are waiting to see whether you drink from it at the next feast.

choices.text: Drink from it, openly

effects.log: You drink. The crack holds. The god who sent it looks away first.

choices.text: Mend the crack with gold and send it back

effects.log: The cup returns better than it went. The hall talks of it for a season.

choices.text: Keep it for your brushes

effects.log: It is a good brush cup. You keep it for the rest of your days, and never say who sent it.

events.text: {ln_order} admits newcomers once a decade, by an old test that is all of forty years old: a scroll in a script nobody on the ground has ever seen, to be read aloud by sunset. {ln_elder} sets down the hourglass and leaves, as if the result were already known.

choices.text: Read it

ok.log: The script is strange, then familiar, as if you had written it once in a dream. You finish before the sand is half run.

fail.log: The letters swim. At sunset you have read the title, which is "Patience".

choices.text: Refuse to be judged by a page

effects.log: You walk out. {ln_elder} writes down the hour you left. It is the only thing written about you.

events.text: The examiners of {ln_court} test the bearing of a newcomer the old way: ask three seated gods for a favour and come back with one. The first god is asleep. The second is {ln_elder}. The third is a goddess of small rains who has never once been asked for anything.

choices.text: Ask {ln_elder}

ok.log: {ln_elder} grants the smallest favour there is, a nod. It counts, and the examiners write it down.

fail.log: {ln_elder} grants nothing, and tells the examiners so, at length.

choices.text: Ask the goddess of small rains

effects.log: The goddess is so pleased that it rains on you all afternoon. It does not count. You are never thirsty there again.

events.text: A test of fortune in {ln_court}: nine sealed doors, one unlocked, and no clue at all. {ln_peer} went first and tried the fifth, and is now sweeping the courtyard for a year. The examiner yawns. The custom is old enough to be cruel and young enough to be changed.

choices.text: Try a door

ok.log: The second door swings open as if it had been waiting for you. The examiner stops yawning.

fail.log: Locked, of course. You join {ln_peer} with a second broom, and the courtyard is very clean.

choices.text: Ask the examiner to change the custom

effects.log: The examiner says no. Next decade the doors have small numbers painted on them, and nobody knows by whom.

events.text: To join {ln_order} a newcomer carries one of the foundation stones of the heaven up its last flight, as the first builders did. The stones were cut from the top of the world below, so you know their weight already: it is the weight of home. {ln_elder} and half the order line the stair to watch.

choices.text: Carry it to the top

ok.log: You set it down at the top without a stagger. Somebody at the back starts to clap and is hushed.

fail.log: Two flights short, your knees decide for you. They roll the stone back down for the next one.

choices.text: Carry it halfway, then sit on it and look at the view

effects.log: You can see all of {b3_world} from there. {ln_elder} comes down to see what you are looking at, and stays.

events.text: An examination in the law of heaven, which in {ln_court} is still being written. The examiner sets you a case: two gods both claim the same sunrise. There is no precedent. There will be one after you answer, and the examiner sharpens a brush to take it down.

choices.text: Divide the sunrise by the hour

ok.log: Your answer goes into the law books, on the first page. You are admitted, and a little famous.

fail.log: The examiner writes it down, then crosses it out. Gods do not care for hours.

choices.text: Say it belongs to the people who wake for it

effects.log: The examiner stops writing. You are not admitted. Down on the ground that year, the sunrises are very fine.

events.text: {ln_elder} has sat in {ln_court} since its floor was laid and does not like the way you walk on it. A circle is chalked on the cloud, and {ln_elder} steps in without taking off a single ring. "Show me what the ground teaches," the old one says. "Then I will show you what it does not."

choices.text: Step into the circle

roll.foeName: The old seated one in the chalk

ok.log: The ground teaches falling, and getting up. You do the second part first. {ln_elder} sits down in the chalk, astonished.

fail.log: {ln_elder} shows you what the ground does not teach. It takes three moves. You remember all three.

choices.text: Bow, and step back from the chalk

effects.log: You bow out. {ln_elder} calls you sensible, which in this heaven is an insult, and a safe one.

events.text: Not a challenge, quite. {ln_elder} simply sits in your chair at the council of {ln_court}, the one with your name freshly painted on the back, and waits. The old seated ones have done this to every newcomer. It is only a chair. It is also everything.

choices.text: Ask for the chair back, the hard way

roll.foeName: The old one in your chair

ok.log: It is a short, polite, dreadful contest. You sit down. Your name dries.

fail.log: You end up on the floor beside the chair, which is where {ln_elder} says newcomers sit.

choices.text: Sit on the floor and speak from there

effects.log: You make the best speech of the council from the floor. Nobody can quite forget where you made it.

events.text: Every newcomer to {ln_court} is put in their place once, by custom, at the edge where the floor ends and the sky drops away to the ground. {ln_elder} has drawn you this year, and says so with real regret: it is nothing personal, it is the custom, and the custom has a fine view.

choices.text: Keep your feet at the edge

roll.foeName: The old one at the edge

ok.log: You hold, and {ln_elder} does not. You catch the old one by the sleeve and pull them back from the drop.

fail.log: You go over the edge, a little. Something catches you. Nobody will admit it was them.

choices.text: Ask why there is such a custom

effects.log: Nobody remembers. It was always so, {ln_elder} says, and then looks troubled at how short always has been.

events.text: {ln_elder} has a student, and the student has a quarrel with you that the student does not yet know about, because {ln_elder} invented it. It is how the old ones of {ln_court} test a newcomer: through a youngster who takes the blame either way. The youngster is shaking with zeal and holding the staff the wrong way round.

choices.text: Walk past the youngster and offer the bout to {ln_elder}

roll.foeName: The old one behind the student

ok.log: The bout is accepted, and lost, by the right one this time.

fail.log: {ln_elder} accepts and wins, and says that is what comes of skipping the queue.

choices.text: Turn the staff the right way round, and lose on purpose

effects.log: The youngster wins and finds out later why. The youngster never forgets it. Nor does {ln_elder}.

events.text: The seated one who keeps the storms of {ln_court} does not challenge you. {ln_elder} simply sends one: a small, personal weather that follows you through the halls for a month and rains on your bed. The other gods are delighted. It is the most heaven has laughed since the floor was laid.

choices.text: Break the storm open

ok.log: You tear it apart with your bare qi. For a day there is a rainbow over your door, and nobody laughs.

fail.log: The storm wins. You are wet a second month, and they laugh for two.

choices.text: Let it rain, and plant a garden under it

effects.log: By spring you have the finest garden in heaven. {ln_elder} calls the storm home, sulking.

events.text: In {ln_court} there is an arch that newcomers do not pass, kept by {ln_elder}, whom nobody ever asked to keep it, and who keeps it anyway, out of habit. You need to go through. {ln_elder} raises one hand to stop you without looking up from a book.

choices.text: Go through regardless

ok.log: The hand does not stop you. {ln_elder} looks up from the book at last, with real interest.

fail.log: The hand stops you, and then sits you down, and then goes back to the book.

choices.text: Ask what the book is

effects.log: It is a book of the songs of the ground. You know three of them. {ln_elder} lets you through for the fourth, and keeps you a week.

events.text: Down on the ground you were {ln_was}, and somebody up here has heard. {ln_elder} asks, with great courtesy, how many people you kept, and says the number back as if it were the age of a child. In {ln_court} a school or a house of the ground is a nursery, and its keeper a nurse.

choices.text: Say the number again, proudly

effects.log: You say it proudly. A few of the younger immortals look at you differently after.

choices.text: Ask how many {ln_elder} keeps

ok.log: None. The silence is very long. You are invited to tea, later, alone.

fail.log: None, and how dare you. You are invited to nothing for a year.

choices.text: Write a long letter down to them instead

effects.log: Below, they read it aloud in the yard. It rains there a little, kindly.

events.text: {ln_was}: that is how you are remembered, and it climbed the stair faster than you did. In {ln_court} the gods have never locked their doors, but they begin to now, one by one, as you pass. {ln_peer} asks you, very quietly, whether the stories are true.

choices.text: Tell {ln_peer} the truth, all of it

effects.log: {ln_peer} goes pale, and stays anyway. One door in heaven, at least, is open.

choices.text: Say the stories are smaller than you are

effects.log: It frightens {ln_peer} more than any story. The doors stay locked, and the gods are very polite.

choices.text: Mend something of the heaven, in daylight

effects.log: You rebuild a broken stair where everyone can watch. The doors stay locked. The stair is used.

events.text: The ground still says your name. Up here it arrives as noise: prayers and petitions rising through the floor of {ln_court}, so many with your name in them that the clerks of the gods have begun a basket for you. {ln_elder} finds the basket, and asks, frostily, who in heaven answers prayers without a seat.

choices.text: Answer them anyway

effects.log: You answer what you can. Down on the ground it is a good harvest. Up here it is a scandal.

choices.text: Give the basket to a seated god

effects.log: The god answers your prayers and takes the thanks. You have a friend in a high place, and a small grudge.

choices.text: Read every one, and answer none

effects.log: It is the best way to know a world, and you know this one now, field by field.

events.text: Nobody below remembers you, and nobody above has heard. {ln_court} does not know where to file you, so for a year you are filed nowhere and live in the gap between the ledgers: no duties, no seat, no rank, and nobody to stop you going anywhere at all.

choices.text: Explore every floor

effects.log: By the end of the year you know heaven better than its gods do. They are a little afraid of that.

choices.text: Ask, politely, to be filed

effects.log: The clerk files you under "other". It is a beginning, of a sort.

choices.text: Make the gap a home

effects.log: You hang a door in the gap. Others with nowhere to be filed start knocking on it.

events.text: A painter of {ln_court} is making a great scroll of the heaven and all its people, and comes to ask who you were. You say: {ln_was}. The painter writes it small, in the margin, beside a sketch of a hill. "The ground is all hills from up here," the painter apologises. "They are hard to tell apart."

choices.text: Describe which hill

effects.log: You describe it until the painter can see it. Yours is the only hill on the scroll with a name.

choices.text: Ask to be painted as you are now

ok.log: The painter moves you from the margin to the edge of the crowd. It is a promotion.

fail.log: The painter tries, sighs and gives up. You are a hill again.

choices.text: Paint the painter

effects.log: Nobody has ever painted the painter before. It is the start of a long friendship.

events.text: The first labour {ln_order} sets a newcomer: sweep the cloud. It does not need sweeping; cloud holds no dust. That is the lesson, {ln_elder} says, and leaves you a broom that looks older than the heaven itself, which nobody here can explain.

choices.text: Sweep it properly, all day

effects.log: You sweep nothing for a whole day, beautifully. {ln_elder} watches from a window and says nothing.

choices.text: Sweep, and ask where the broom came from

effects.log: It came up the stair with the first god, who cannot remember carrying it. You keep asking. You keep sweeping.

events.text: {ln_order} sets you to copy its register of members in a fair hand. The register is short, the heaven being young, and you notice that the very first name in it is written in a hand much like your own. Nobody else has noticed. It may be nothing. It is almost certainly not nothing.

choices.text: Copy it faithfully, and say nothing

effects.log: The copy is perfect. You leave the first name for last, and your brush shakes on it.

choices.text: Copy it, and ask about the first name

effects.log: Nobody knows who wrote it. {ln_elder} looks at it a long while, then at you, then away.

events.text: A labour for {ln_order}: carry messages between its hall and the next one, which are not speaking. Each message is rude. Each is longer than the last. On the third day you understand that both halls are waiting for you to soften them, and that neither will ever say so.

choices.text: Carry them word for word

effects.log: The feud goes on. You are praised for honesty by both sides, who agree on nothing else.

choices.text: Soften them, a word at a time

ok.log: By the tenth message they are inviting each other to dinner, and blaming you for it.

fail.log: One hall notices. The labour counts, barely, and you are watched after.

events.text: {ln_order} sets a newcomer to tend the lamps along the stair down to the ground, the long stair you climbed. Far below, at the very bottom, somebody has left a lamp lit every night since you went up. You can just see it if you lean out, a pinprick in the dark.

choices.text: Tend the lamps, and lean out each night

effects.log: The lamps of the stair have never burned brighter. Nor has the pinprick.

choices.text: Tend them all the way down, and carry a light to the bottom

effects.log: You are three days late back, and it counts. Below, somebody stops leaving the lamp, because you came.

events.text: The last labour {ln_order} sets is to sit with its oldest member, who is fading, as gods here sometimes do, quietly and without fuss. The old god wants no comfort. The old god wants to be told what the ground is like now, because nobody has asked in a hundred years.

choices.text: Tell it all, the good and the bad

effects.log: You talk until morning. The old god laughs twice, and goes, and the order is gentler with you after.

choices.text: Tell only the good

effects.log: The old god knows, and is grateful anyway, and holds your hand at the end.

choices.text: Bring a handful of soil from below

effects.log: You bring it up the whole stair in a cloth. The old god holds it to the last.

events.text: The examination hall empties into the courtyard, and three hundred young people try not to look at the gate where the list will go up. Beside you {ln_peer} recites answers aloud, the right ones, a day too late. A porter comes out with a ladder and a pot of paste, and takes all the time in the world.

choices.text: Read the list from the top

effects.log: Your name is wherever it is. You read the rest as well, and remember who wept.

choices.text: Read the list from the bottom up

effects.log: Every name you pass, you are glad for. It is a good way to read a list, whatever it says.

choices.text: Take {ln_peer} for a drink first

effects.log: Whatever the list says, you remember that drink for longer.

events.text: After the examination the old proctor of the academy finds you in the corridor and hands back a brush you left behind. "You held it like a farmer," the proctor says. "Farmers make good scholars. They know about waiting." And is gone before you can ask whether that was praise or a warning.

choices.text: Keep the brush for luck

effects.log: You keep it. It does not change the result. It changes how you carry it.

choices.text: Run after the proctor

ok.log: The proctor tells you which question you answered best. It was the one you nearly left blank.

fail.log: The proctor is very quick for someone so old. You lose the trail by the library.

events.text: Results day, and whatever the board says about you, the town below the academy has made a fair of it: dumpling sellers, fortune-tellers, and somebody selling "the true answers" a day late, at half price. A fortune-teller catches your sleeve and offers to tell you whether you ought to be happy.

choices.text: Pay for a fortune

effects.log: The fortune-teller says you will be happy, in time. It is the cheapest true thing in town.

choices.text: Buy the true answers, for the joke

effects.log: Three of them are wrong. You are oddly comforted.

choices.text: Walk through it all with empty hands

effects.log: You buy nothing and eat nothing and enjoy it anyway, which is its own small skill.

events.text: Word comes up the stair, as word does: down on the ground, {npc} is being called the upstart's leftover. Neighbours who once borrowed salt now say {he} married a ladder. The gods of {ln_court} hear it through the floor, find it very funny, and repeat it within your hearing.

choices.text: Speak for {npc} before the gods

effects.log: You tell the hall exactly who {npc} is. It costs you up here. Down below, somehow, {npc} hears of it.

choices.text: Send {npc} a letter and a gift with your seal

effects.log: The gift arrives with your seal on it. The neighbours start borrowing salt again.

choices.text: Let it pass

effects.log: You let it pass. So does {npc}. You both feel the distance grow, a stair wide.

events.text: {npc}, who is yours down on the ground, has been turned away from the county temple. The priest said the kin of one who climbed up and never came back must think themselves too good for prayer. It is a small cruelty, and up here it is told as a joke about how the dust still clings to you.

choices.text: Vouch for {npc} at the rail where the prayers come up

effects.log: You speak for {npc} where the gods can hear. They think less of you. Below, the temple door opens.

choices.text: Send the priest a dream

ok.log: The priest wakes up very sorry, and gives {npc} the front row.

fail.log: The dream reaches the wrong priest, two counties away, who is now very confused.

choices.text: Write to {npc} that you are proud

effects.log: The letter lives in {his} sleeve after that. {He} reads it to the priest, twice.

events.text: {npc}, who learned from you on the ground, is being mocked in the market: the pupil of one who ran up the sky and left {him} with half a lesson. Rival schools send their youngest to jeer at {his} gate. Up here {ln_elder} hears of it, and remarks that a teacher of dust can only make more dust.

choices.text: Answer {ln_elder}, for {npc}

effects.log: You say {npc} is worth any three pupils of this heaven. It goes badly for you, and well for {him}.

choices.text: Send {npc} the other half of the lesson

effects.log: You write it out in full and send it down. The jeering stops the day {npc} uses it.

choices.text: Trust {npc} to answer for {him}self

effects.log: You trust. It is hard. {npc} answers the jeering alone, and better than you would have.

events.text: {npc}, an old friend from the ground, has been thrown out of a tavern for claiming to know you. Everybody claims to know the ones who went up, the keeper said; next {he} will say {he} lent you money. {npc} did lend you money, and in {ln_court} it is the best joke of the season.

choices.text: Vouch for {npc} in heaven, aloud

effects.log: You say {npc} lent you money, and more than money. The gods laugh harder. You find you do not care.

choices.text: Repay the loan, with interest

effects.log: The money arrives at the tavern itself. The keeper buys {npc} a drink every week for a year.

choices.text: Laugh along with them

effects.log: You laugh too. It is easier. It sits badly with you for a long while after.

events.text: One morning in {ln_court} the clerk who once wrote "from below" beside your name crosses it out, unasked, and writes nothing in its place. {ln_elder} passes you on the stair and gives the nod the old ones give each other. Nobody says you have landed. That is how you know.

choices.text: Nod back

effects.log: You nod back. It is the shortest and the longest conversation of your life.

choices.text: Go and meet the next newcomer at the door

effects.log: You walk the newcomer in from the top of the stair. Nobody did it for you. Somebody should have.

events.text: You are seated at the feast tonight, not at the end, though you choose to sit beside the river god anyway. The heaven is a little older now, and so are its floors. They no longer give underfoot as they did. They have been walked on enough, and some of the walking was yours.

choices.text: Raise a cup to the river god

effects.log: The river god weeps a little into the cup. Somewhere below, a dry bed runs again for a week.

choices.text: Raise a cup to the ground

effects.log: The hall goes quiet, then raises its cups too. Far below, a field you knew has a good year.

events.text: A newcomer arrives in {ln_court} looking exactly as you once did: dust to the knee, and a name that means something only down there. The gods along the rail look to you now, to see what you will do. It turns out you are one of them. It turns out that is a choice.

choices.text: Look down on the newcomer, as is done

effects.log: You do it once, as is done. It feels like a borrowed coat that does not fit.

choices.text: Go down the rail and say welcome

effects.log: You say it. The rail is scandalised. The newcomer will remember it for a thousand years.

choices.text: Watch, and say nothing

effects.log: You watch the newcomer climb into heaven the way you did. It is harder to watch from up here.

events.text: The doorkeeper of the Lantern Gallery in {ln_court} names you a price. It is a third more than the immortal ahead of you paid, who belongs to a house. You say so. The doorkeeper points to a small sign: "No house, no school, no seat: see price." The paint on the sign is still wet.

choices.text: Pay the price

effects.log: Inside hang lanterns for every life this world has lived. One of them, oddly, looks like yours.

choices.text: Haggle

ok.log: The doorkeeper lets you in at the house price, and denies it to everyone after.

fail.log: The price goes up for arguing, and the queue enjoys it.

choices.text: Walk on

effects.log: You walk on. The sign stays, and so does the price, for the next one.

events.text: A tavern of the heaven's immortals keeps a back room for those of no house. It is, you discover, also the storeroom. You sit among the barrels, over tea, with {ln_peer}, also of no house, and a lesser god who once resigned a seat and now cannot get it back.

choices.text: Make it the best room in the tavern

effects.log: By the end of the season the front room is jealous, and the barrels are very well attended.

choices.text: Ask the lesser god what happened

effects.log: The story is long and sad and very funny. You learn exactly how a seat is lost.

choices.text: Leave a coin on the barrel

effects.log: The keeper starts saving you the good stool, the one that does not wobble.

events.text: A school of {ln_court} shuts its door in your face: not rudely, just firmly, the way one shuts out weather. You were not even going to ask to join. You were going to ask the way to the library. A child of the school opens an upstairs window and points.

choices.text: Thank the child

effects.log: The child waves until you are out of sight, and is scolded, and does it again next time.

choices.text: Knock again and ask to join after all

effects.log: They say no again, at greater length. It is, in its way, educational.

choices.text: Find the library on your own

effects.log: It takes three days. The library has no door at all, and is kinder for it.

events.text: Down on the ground a village still prays to you. It does not know you went up, nor that you are nobody here. Each evening its small prayers rise through the floor of {ln_court} and land at your feet like moths. A seated god, passing, asks why one with no seat is getting post.

choices.text: Answer the village anyway

effects.log: You answer as a seatless one can: a little rain, a found goat. The village rejoices. The seated god does not.

choices.text: Let the seated god answer them

effects.log: The god answers coolly, and is thanked. You feel it go, like a coat lifted off your back.

choices.text: Keep the prayers in a jar

effects.log: You keep them by your bed. On bad nights you lift the lid and listen to them.

events.text: The market of {ln_court} has a separate queue for those with no house, no school and no seat. It moves when the other queue is empty. The other queue is never empty. A fruit-seller who came up from the ground three hundred years ago catches your eye and nods toward the back of the stall.

choices.text: Go round the back

effects.log: You buy at the back, at the prices of the ground. You do not tell anyone, and nor does the fruit-seller.

choices.text: Stand in the queue, on principle

effects.log: You stand all day. By evening three others stand with you, and the queue is slightly famous.

choices.text: Pay the front of the stall to serve you

effects.log: They serve you, for a third more, with a smile that costs extra.

events.text: {ln_order} is holding a lecture on the making of the world, the first ever given in this heaven, and at the door you are told it is for members. You can hear it from the corridor. The speaker has the story of the making almost right, and keeps stopping just where you would have gone on.

choices.text: Listen from the corridor

effects.log: You learn how the gods think the world was made. It is wrong in ways that feel personal.

choices.text: Correct the speaker, from the corridor

ok.log: The speaker stops, then asks you in. Not as a member: as a source.

fail.log: They close the corridor door as well.

choices.text: Go and look at the world itself instead

effects.log: You stand at the edge and look down at it for an hour. It is the better lecture.

events.text: No inn in {ln_court} will lodge one without a house at the house rate. The keeper of the Floating Gate offers a room at a quarter more, or the stable for nothing, where the cloud-horses sleep and the hay is a little damp. The stable, the keeper says, is very popular with philosophers.

choices.text: Take the room

effects.log: The bed is soft. The bill is not.

choices.text: Take the stable

effects.log: By morning you are a philosopher. The horses have views, and share them.

choices.text: Sleep on the open cloud under the stars

effects.log: It is cold and enormous and quiet. You have never slept better, nor woken stiffer.

events.text: Two gods of {ln_court} are marrying, and the guests are ranked by school and house. Those with neither stand behind the musicians, where the wedding can be seen only in the polished back of a drum. The drummer has noticed, and plays a little to the left so that you can see.

choices.text: Thank the drummer afterwards

effects.log: The drummer becomes a friend. Drummers know everything that happens in a heaven.

choices.text: Leave a gift anyway

effects.log: Yours is the only gift the couple remember, being the only one with no seal on it.

choices.text: Watch it all in the drum

effects.log: It is a lovely wedding, slightly curved.

events.text: A herald of {ln_court} is counting the people of the heaven, with a column for school, a column for house and a column for seat. For you the herald writes three dashes, and then, being young and honest, a fourth dash in a column that does not exist.

choices.text: Ask what the fourth dash means

effects.log: The herald says it means "and yet here". It is the best thing anyone has written about you.

choices.text: Suggest a column called "self"

ok.log: The column is added at the next count. It is very long.

fail.log: The herald says the count is no place for jokes, and adds a fifth dash.

events.text: To wander {ln_court} is to belong to no floor of it. You take up the road with a staff and a blank book, and on the first night at the edge of the cloud you meet the Lamplighter, an old wanderer who walks the unfinished rim lighting lamps nobody asked for. "The map ends here," the Lamplighter says. "Nobody has drawn the rest."

choices.text: Walk the rim with the Lamplighter

effects.log: You walk all night. By dawn you have a companion, of a sort, and the first page of your book.

choices.text: Begin drawing the map yourself

effects.log: You draw the rim as far as you can see. The page ends before the rim does.

events.text: The Lamplighter shows you a floor of {ln_court} that is only half laid: stone to the middle, then scaffolding, then sky. Nobody works here. Tools lie where they were put down long ago, by somebody who meant to come back. The chisels fit your hand. They fit it rather too well.

choices.text: Pick up a chisel and cut one stone

effects.log: You cut it without thinking, in a style nobody in heaven uses. The Lamplighter goes very quiet.

choices.text: Leave the tools as they lie

effects.log: Some things should wait for whoever put them down. You mark the place in your book.

events.text: Wanderers are not welcome at the tables of the gods, but every heaven needs messages carried between floors that do not speak. For a year you are the courier of {ln_court}, trusted because you belong to nobody. A seated god hands you a letter for a rival, and the letter is warm: the first warm thing between them in a century.

choices.text: Deliver it, unread

effects.log: The rival reads it twice. Two floors of heaven begin speaking again, and nobody knows it was you.

choices.text: Read it first, then deliver it

effects.log: It is a love letter, very old. You keep the secret, and the god who wrote it knows you kept it.

events.text: The Lamplighter is ill, the way old wanderers grow ill: thinning, like mist at noon. With no seat, no school and no house, nobody in {ln_court} will take the old one in. You carry the Lamplighter from door to door along the rim, and the doors are polite, and shut.

choices.text: Pay a hall to take the Lamplighter in

effects.log: A hall takes the money and the Lamplighter, at the price for those with no backing. The bed is warm.

choices.text: Build a shelter on the half-laid floor

effects.log: You build it with the old tools. They know the work better than you do. The Lamplighter sleeps.

events.text: In the Lamplighter's pack, while the old one sleeps, you find a map: the rim of the heaven drawn far beyond your own, in a hand that changes over the years from steady to shaking. On the last page is a door with no wall around it, and a note: "Not mine to open. Theirs, when they come."

choices.text: Ask the Lamplighter whose door it is

effects.log: The Lamplighter smiles and will not say. "You will know it when you are standing at it."

choices.text: Copy the old map into your own book

effects.log: Page by page, the two books become one book, and the rim runs almost to the end of it.

events.text: The Lamplighter dies, or thins out entirely, which in {ln_court} is the same thing done more gently. There is no school to bury a wanderer and no house to mourn one. There are only the lamps along the rim, which go out one by one on the nights after, unless somebody walks the rim and lights them.

choices.text: Walk the rim and light the lamps

effects.log: It takes a month. Somewhere in the month it stops being the old one's work and becomes yours.

choices.text: Let them go dark, and grieve

effects.log: You sit in the dark a long while. When you rise, you know the way by feel.

events.text: At the far end of the rim, past the last lamp, stands the door from the map: a door with no wall, open onto nothing. On its frame, in chalk, somebody long ago drew the plan of the whole heaven of {b3_world}, floor by floor. The hand is your hand. You are not surprised, and that surprises you most of all.

choices.text: Close it gently and walk back along the rim

effects.log: You go home by the lamps, all lit. Wanderers come to you now, and you tell them the way.

choices.text: Add one line to the plan

effects.log: You draw one more room, small, at the edge: a room for those with no seat. When you look back, it is there.

choices.text: Sit on the threshold until morning

effects.log: You sit between heaven and nothing all night, and come away lighter, and older, and not tired.
